question: Sustained positive G (acting head-to-foot, as in a tightening turn or pull-up) primarily stresses the body by:

options.text: Pooling blood toward the lower body, reducing blood flow and pressure available to the brain and eyes
Pushing blood toward the head, risking a stroke from excess pressure
Having no effect on blood distribution at all
Only affecting the inner ear, not the cardiovascular system

explanation: Positive G effectively increases the weight of blood, pulling it toward the feet and away from the head. As cardiovascular compensation is overwhelmed, vision is the first system to suffer (greyout, then blackout) followed, at higher G, by loss of consciousness (G-LOC).

question: "Greyout" under positive G describes:

options.text: A progressive loss of peripheral, then central, vision as blood pressure to the eyes falls, while consciousness is still retained
Complete loss of consciousness
A loss of hearing that precedes any visual symptom
A condition that only occurs under negative G

explanation: Vision is particularly sensitive to reduced blood pressure because the retina has a high metabolic demand. Greyout (dimming, narrowing field of view) typically precedes blackout (total vision loss) which, if G continues to increase, can be followed by G-induced loss of consciousness.

question: Negative G (acting foot-to-head) can cause "redout", which is best described as:

options.text: A reddish tint or haemorrhage-related visual disturbance caused by blood being forced toward the head and eyes
The same phenomenon as greyout, just under a different name
A sensation limited to the inner ear with no visual component
A condition that only affects colour vision, not brightness

explanation: Negative G reverses the direction of blood pooling compared with positive G, forcing blood toward the head and eyes instead of away from them, which can produce a reddish visual disturbance rather than the dimming seen under positive G.

question: A given level of G is far better tolerated when applied only briefly (an impulse, such as hitting turbulence) than when sustained for several seconds, mainly because:

options.text: Sustained G gives the cardiovascular system time to be overwhelmed as blood is progressively redistributed, while a brief impulse does not allow enough time for that redistribution
Brief G has no physical effect on the body at all
Sustained G is always lower in magnitude than impulse G
The body's tolerance to G has nothing to do with duration

explanation: It takes a certain amount of time for blood to actually shift and for blood pressure at the eyes and brain to drop meaningfully. A short, sharp G spike can be well tolerated even at a magnitude that would cause blackout if sustained for several seconds.

question: Which factor would reduce an individual's tolerance to sustained positive G?

options.text: Fatigue, dehydration, or being unfit
Being well hydrated and rested
Regular physical conditioning of the legs and abdomen
Wearing a properly fitted anti-G garment

explanation: Fatigue, dehydration and poor physical conditioning all reduce the cardiovascular system's ability to compensate for G-induced blood pooling, lowering the G level at which greyout or blackout begins. Conditioning and anti-G equipment work the other way, raising tolerance.

question: Barotrauma affecting the sinuses or middle ear during a descent is governed most directly by:

options.text: Boyle's Law — trapped gas in an enclosed space expands as ambient pressure falls, and must contract again as pressure rises on descent, straining tissue if it cannot vent freely
Dalton's Law of partial pressures
Charles' Law of temperature and volume
A purely psychological effect with no physical cause

explanation: Air trapped in a sinus or the middle ear behaves according to Boyle's Law: at constant temperature its volume varies inversely with pressure. If a blocked passage (from a cold, for example) prevents that trapped air from equalizing with the changing cabin pressure, the tissue around it bears the strain.

question: A pilot with a head cold and blocked sinuses is generally advised against flying mainly because:

options.text: Blocked passages prevent trapped gas from equalizing smoothly with cabin pressure changes, risking painful barotrauma, particularly on descent
A cold has no bearing on barotrauma risk
Flying always cures a head cold
The risk only exists on the climb, never on the descent

explanation: Descent is usually the more problematic direction, because the relatively higher ambient pressure needs to push air back into the sinuses or middle ear through a passage that congestion has already narrowed or blocked, which is exactly when pain and even injury can occur.

question: Body Mass Index (BMI) is calculated from:

options.text: Body mass divided by the square of height
Height divided by body mass
Body mass multiplied by age
Waist circumference divided by height

explanation: BMI is defined as mass (kg) divided by height squared (m²). It is a simple screening measure of weight relative to height, not a direct measure of body fat, and is interpreted alongside other health indicators rather than alone.

question: Obesity is relevant to a pilot's medical fitness mainly because it is associated with increased risk of:

options.text: Cardiovascular disease, diabetes and sleep apnoea, each of which can affect in-flight performance or sudden incapacitation risk
Improved G tolerance in every case
No measurable health risk of any kind
Colour blindness

explanation: Obesity raises the risk of several conditions directly relevant to flight safety — cardiovascular disease and sudden incapacitation risk, diabetes and its effect on alertness, and sleep apnoea's effect on daytime fatigue — which is why weight is reviewed as part of ongoing medical fitness.

question: On a multi-crew flight, it is common practice for the captain and first officer to eat different meal options before or during a flight mainly to:

options.text: Reduce the chance that both pilots are simultaneously incapacitated by food poisoning from the same contaminated meal
Save money for the operator
Comply with a requirement that has nothing to do with safety
Allow each pilot to try new foods

explanation: If both pilots ate the same, contaminated meal, food poisoning could incapacitate them both at the same time with no one fit to fly. Eating different meals is a simple, low-cost way to keep that specific risk from affecting the whole crew at once.

question: A simple faint (vasovagal syncope) differs from an epileptic fit mainly in that a faint:

options.text: Is usually preceded by warning signs (light-headedness, pallor, sweating) and involves a brief, self-limiting drop in blood pressure and blood flow to the brain, typically with rapid recovery once lying flat
Always involves convulsive muscle movements lasting several minutes
Is caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain
Never has any warning signs at all

explanation: A faint is typically a vascular event — blood pressure drops, often with clear warning symptoms, and recovery is usually quick once blood flow to the brain is restored (for example, by lying down). A seizure, by contrast, arises from abnormal brain electrical activity and often includes convulsive movement and a longer recovery.

question: Alcohol impairs flying performance at blood concentrations well below the level associated with obvious outward drunkenness mainly because it:

options.text: Degrades judgement, reaction time and complex decision-making before any visible loss of coordination appears
Only affects physical coordination, never mental performance
Has no measurable effect below the level that produces visible drunkenness
Improves reaction time at low doses

explanation: Higher mental functions — judgement, risk assessment, multitasking — are impaired by alcohol at lower concentrations than those needed to produce obviously slurred speech or unsteady movement, which is exactly why "feeling fine" is not a reliable test of fitness to fly.

question: The body eliminates alcohol from the bloodstream at a roughly steady rate over time, which means:

options.text: Drinking strong coffee, taking a cold shower or any other "quick fix" does not meaningfully speed up how fast blood alcohol actually falls
Alcohol is eliminated instantly once a person stops drinking
Coffee chemically breaks down alcohol in the stomach
A cold shower lowers blood alcohol concentration directly

explanation: The liver metabolises alcohol at a roughly constant rate regardless of what else is done. Common folk remedies may make a person feel more alert, but they do nothing to change the actual rate at which blood alcohol concentration falls — only time does that.

question: Alcohol consumed the evening before an early flight can still impair performance the next morning even if blood alcohol itself has returned to zero, because:

options.text: Byproducts of alcohol metabolism and disrupted sleep quality can leave a "hangover" effect on alertness and judgement well after the alcohol itself is gone
Alcohol permanently reduces cognitive ability after a single use
Zero blood alcohol always means zero impairment, with no exceptions
Hangover effects are purely psychological, with no measurable effect on performance

explanation: Alcohol disrupts normal sleep architecture and leaves metabolic byproducts that can affect how a person feels and performs well after blood alcohol concentration itself has reached zero — which is why a measured zero reading does not automatically mean a person is fully fit to fly.

question: A common, easily overlooked risk with over-the-counter medications (such as some antihistamines or cold remedies) and flying is that:

options.text: Many cause drowsiness or slowed reaction time as a side effect, even though they are freely available without a prescription
Over-the-counter medications are guaranteed to have no effect on flying performance
Only prescription drugs can ever affect flying performance
They are automatically banned from being carried on an aircraft

explanation: Being available without a prescription does not mean a medication is free of side effects relevant to flying. Many common cold and allergy remedies cause drowsiness or slowed reactions, which is exactly the kind of impairment self-medication can introduce without a pilot realising it.

question: The safest general approach for a pilot considering any new medication, prescribed or otherwise, is to:

options.text: Check its effects and interactions before flying, and if in doubt, not fly until the medication's effects are known and have been assessed as compatible with flying duties
Assume all medications are safe to fly on immediately after the first dose
Take a double dose before a flight to ensure the medical condition is fully controlled
Rely solely on how alert they personally feel after taking it

explanation: Individual responses to a new medication are not always predictable from the leaflet alone, and personal judgement about feeling alert is not a reliable self-test. The standard caution is to know the medication's known effects and, if any doubt remains, not to fly.

question: Beyond carbon monoxide from a faulty exhaust or heater, a buildup of carbon dioxide in a poorly ventilated cabin or cockpit mainly causes:

options.text: Headache, drowsiness and impaired performance, worsening with concentration and exposure time
No effect at all, since carbon dioxide is physiologically inert
An immediate improvement in alertness
A permanent change in blood type

explanation: Even without a toxic gas like carbon monoxide present, inadequate ventilation can allow exhaled carbon dioxide to build up, which at raised concentrations causes headache, drowsiness and declining mental performance — a straightforward reason good cabin ventilation matters.

question: Cosmic radiation exposure for aircrew generally increases with:

options.text: Increasing altitude and increasing latitude
Decreasing altitude only
Flying exclusively near the equator
Time of day, regardless of altitude or route

explanation: The atmosphere shields less cosmic radiation at higher altitude, and the Earth's magnetic field channels more of it toward the poles, so exposure rises both with cruising altitude and with the latitude of the route flown — long polar routes at high altitude see the greatest exposure.

question: Cosmic radiation exposure is managed for long-haul aircrew mainly by:

options.text: Monitoring and limiting cumulative exposure over time, since no practical cockpit shielding exists against it
Fitting lead shielding around the cockpit
Flying lower rather than higher whenever possible, with no other measure needed
Ignoring it entirely, since it has no cumulative effect

explanation: There is no practical way to shield an aircraft cockpit from cosmic radiation the way a hospital shields an X-ray room. Instead, exposure is estimated by route and altitude and managed as a cumulative, tracked occupational exposure, similar in principle to other radiation workers.

question: The "stroboscopic effect", in which a rotating propeller or rotor can momentarily appear to be stationary or turning unusually slowly, is caused by:

options.text: A coincidence between the rotational speed and a flickering light source (such as certain artificial lighting), which effectively samples the blade position at a matching rate
A genuine, physical slowing of the propeller caused by the light itself
A problem with the pilot's eyesight rather than with lighting
An effect that can only happen in bright, continuous sunlight

explanation: If a flickering light source happens to pulse at close to the blade's rotational frequency, each flash can catch the blade in nearly the same position, creating a visual illusion that it is barely moving or standing still — a genuine hazard around a propeller that is, in reality, still turning at speed.

question: Good personal hygiene is relevant to flight safety mainly because:

options.text: Poor hygiene increases the risk of minor infections and illness that could affect fitness to fly, and in a shared crew environment can spread illness to others
It has no bearing on flight safety whatsoever
It is relevant only to cabin crew, never to pilots
It only matters for appearance, not health

explanation: Hygiene affects both an individual's own risk of minor illness (which can affect fitness to fly) and the risk of passing an infection on to other crew in a shared, confined working environment — making it more than a purely cosmetic consideration.

question: Regular physical exercise benefits a pilot's performance partly by:

options.text: Improving cardiovascular fitness, which can raise tolerance to physical stressors including sustained G and general fatigue resistance
Having no measurable effect on any aspect of flying performance
Reducing the need for sleep entirely
Eliminating the need for a balanced diet

explanation: Better cardiovascular conditioning improves the body's ability to maintain blood pressure to the brain under physical stress, including sustained G, and generally supports greater resilience to fatigue over a demanding duty day.

subtopic: Common ailments and fitness to fly
question: A pilot who feels generally unwell but is not sure whether the condition is serious enough to affect flying is best guided by the principle that:

options.text: If there is genuine doubt about fitness to fly, the safer choice is not to fly, or to seek medical advice before doing so
Minor symptoms can always be safely ignored once airborne
Only symptoms that are visible to others are worth considering
A pilot should always fly as scheduled regardless of how they feel

explanation: The "if in doubt, don't" principle used for fitness to fly mirrors the one used for medication: the consequences of flying while genuinely unfit outweigh the inconvenience of delaying or seeking advice first.

question: A sudden, otherwise unexplained headache, drowsiness or nausea affecting more than one occupant of a small aircraft with a cabin heater in use should prompt a pilot to suspect:

options.text: Possible carbon monoxide contamination from the heating or exhaust system, and to take immediate action such as shutting off the heater and ventilating the cabin
A simple coincidence with no common cause worth investigating
Motion sickness alone, regardless of how many people are affected
A problem that can safely wait until after landing to address

explanation: Several occupants becoming unwell at the same time, especially with a cabin heater drawing air near the exhaust in use, is a recognised warning sign of carbon monoxide ingress, and standard guidance is to shut off the source, ventilate immediately and treat it as urgent rather than coincidental.
